name: Undercut / fade with textured top

image.caption: Paul De La Cruz pauldlc undercut hair style

lead: A short faded side and back with a longer, textured top gives a clean outline and volume on top, and a skin fade is said to make the face and jaw look sharper.

The undercut dates to early 20th-century working-class men, was mainstream in the 1920s and 1930s and revived in the early 2010s, with adopters such as David Beckham. It is frequently cited in men's grooming advice as a flattering cut for many face shapes; those claims come from stylists and forums, not studies.

paras: People ask a barber for a fade or tapered sides and keep length on top, then style it with matte clay or paste for texture. It needs a trim every few weeks to keep the fade sharp, and the new look shows straight away.
Low risk. Maintenance is frequent, and the look needs enough hair on top to style.

angle.text: Short faded sides with a longer styled top give a clean outline and volume, and a skin fade is said to make the face and jaw look sharper. The haircut change is visible immediately and the style is widely recommended for many face shapes.

lead: The undercut with a fade and textured top is a men's haircut in which the sides and back are clipped very short, often tapering gradually to the skin, while the top stays long enough to style. People choose it to change the shape of the head and face: the clean, tight sides draw attention to the jaw, cheekbones and eyes, and the volume on top adds apparent height and frames the forehead. A textured top means the longer hair is styled with product for body and a matte, tousled finish rather than a flat slick look [1].

Wikipedia describes the undercut as short back and sides with longer hair on top, usually parted to the side or centre. It was fashionable from the 1910s to the 1940s, revived in the 1980s and became popular again in the 2010s, when the top was often swept back or to one side with pomade or gel [1]. Early-2010s adopters listed by Wikipedia include David Beckham and Macklemore [1]. A fade is a tapered version of the short sides, in which the clippers blend from shorter hair at the bottom to longer hair above; Wikipedia's haircut article lists 'fade' as another name for the short taper cut [2].

No published study has tested whether this cut changes how attractive someone is rated. On looksmax.org, hairstyle choice is discussed as a quick appearance change, and opinions on the undercut vary [3].
infobox: Short or faded sides and back, longer styled top [1]

paras: The undercut shaves or buzzes the back and sides and leaves longer hair on top [1]. A fade creates a gradual taper on the sides, with the clippers gradually arced out from the head as they move up [2]. Wikipedia's article on the 2010s version notes the top was often swept back or to one side with pomade or gel [1].

sections.h: How people use it to look better
paras: Short sides take bulk away from the sides of the head, so the face reads as longer and the jaw and cheekbones show more clearly. Contrast between the sides and a fuller top adds height, a reason people with thick hair or a wish to look taller choose it. Stylists and forum users also describe it as a way to shift attention away from the forehead or a rounder jaw; these recommendations by face shape are opinion rather than research findings.

Wikipedia associates the undercut with working-class youth and street gangs in the early 1900s, a fashionable status from the 1910s to the 1940s, a decline as longer styles took over in the 1960s, and revivals among new wave fans in the late 1980s and among hipsters and others in the 2010s [1]. Variants listed include the centrally parted version, the curtained style and the slicked-back style [1]. Wikipedia also records that the undercut was common among German soldiers in World War II and that short back-and-sides cuts became the norm for professional men by about 1910 [2].

A looksmax.org thread asks whether a disconnected undercut is a good method for looksmaxxing; the original poster, who has thick hair, says many people including celebrities wear it and wants to see if it improves their look [3]. Replies in that thread were mixed, with one describing the style as common and another saying it suits only certain public figures [3].
